content: The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation recommends the use of both short-acting and long-acting insulin therapy for individuals diagnosed with cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD). The diagnosis of CFRD is based on specific criteria: fasting blood glucose levels exceeding 6.94 mmol/L (125 mg/dL), oral glucose tolerance test results greater than 11.11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) at two hours, random glucose levels above 11.11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) in the presence of diabetes symptoms, or glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels of at least 6.5%. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of insulin and oral hypoglycemic agents in managing CFRD, specifically in terms of blood glucose control, lung function, and weight management. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing various pharmacological treatments for CFRD. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, including electronic databases, handsearches of journals, conference abstracts, and online trial registries. The most recent searches were conducted in September 2020. The review identified 29 trials, of which four provided usable data. These included: 1. A short-term, single-center crossover trial involving seven adults with CFRD and normal fasting glucose, comparing insulin, oral repaglinide, and no medication. 2. A long-term, multicenter trial with 61 adults comparing insulin, oral repaglinide, and placebo. 3. Another long-term, multicenter trial with 67 adults comparing insulin and oral repaglinide. 4. A 12-week, single-center crossover trial with 20 adults comparing long-acting insulin glargine to short-acting neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin. Two ongoing trials investigating newly approved incretin mimetics were also noted for potential future inclusion. The quality of evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias, particularly related to allocation concealment and selective reporting, as well as imprecision from small sample sizes and low event rates. Additionally, there were concerns about the comparability of insulin and repaglinide dosages. In one trial comparing insulin to placebo (39 participants), no significant differences were observed in blood glucose levels (very low-quality evidence), lung function (low-quality evidence), or nutritional status (low-quality evidence). Similarly, no differences were found in secondary outcomes such as hypoglycemic episodes, secondary infection complications, or quality of life (QoL). These findings were consistent with narrative reports from a second trial in this comparison (seven participants). A one-year trial comparing repaglinide to placebo (38 participants) also showed no differences in blood glucose levels, lung function, or nutritional status (all very low-quality evidence). Secondary outcomes, including hypoglycemic episodes, secondary infections, and QoL, were similarly unaffected. These results were mirrored in narrative reports from a second trial (seven participants). Three trials compared insulin to repaglinide (119 participants). One trial (67 participants) found no differences in blood glucose levels at 12 or 24 months (high-quality evidence). Narrative reports from another trial (45 participants) also found no differences, while a third trial (seven participants) suggested a potential benefit of insulin over repaglinide. Two trials (112 participants) found no differences in lung function or nutritional status (moderate-quality evidence). Two trials (56 participants) reported no differences in hypoglycemic episodes (low-quality evidence). One trial (45 participants) found no differences in secondary infections or QoL. A single trial comparing glargine to NPH insulin did not directly assess the primary outcomes of the review but reported no differences in postprandial glucose levels or weight. Neither group experienced infectious complications. There were no differences in hypoglycemic episodes (very low-quality evidence) or QoL, although all participants chose to continue glargine treatment after the trial. Mortality was not reported in any trial, and no deaths were cited as reasons for withdrawal. The authors concluded that there is no conclusive evidence to suggest that any specific pharmacological agent has a clear advantage over others in managing hyperglycemia or improving clinical outcomes in CFRD. Given the significant treatment burden faced by individuals with cystic fibrosis, oral therapies may be a viable option. However, the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation's clinical practice guidelines continue to recommend insulin therapy, which remains the most widely used treatment. Future RCTs should focus on the impact of diabetes control on pulmonary disease progression in cystic fibrosis, adherence to different therapies, and the potential benefits of additional hypoglycemic agents, including incretin mimetics. Agents that enhance insulin action, particularly those with anti-inflammatory properties, should also be explored as adjunctive therapies to insulin.
